title: "The mind is restless" — Arjuna admits it (6.29–6.36)
hook: after all the instructions, Arjuna says what everyone is thinking: this is impossible

segments.voice: Yesterday: dipa, the lamp in a windless place. Your line was flame unwavering. How many times did you bring your attention back? If the answer is a lot, today's reading is for you. Day one hundred eighty-one.

You sit down to be still. Ten seconds in, you're thinking about lunch. Then an email. Then a conversation from 2014 that you lost, and how you should have answered. Then lunch again. Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the self in every being and the lamp that doesn't flicker. And Arjuna, a warrior whose whole craft is a steady aim, stops him and says, basically: I can't do this. My mind won't hold still.
screen: `TEN SECONDS IN: LUNCH.` → `THEN A CONVERSATION FROM 2014.` → `ARJUNA: I CAN'T DO THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the vision that sets Arjuna off. The yogi, verse twenty-nine says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. And the highest yogi, verse thirty-two, is the one who looks at another's joy or pain as if it were their own. Beautiful. And Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you describe, I don't see how it can last, because the mind is restless. Then verse thirty-four, said plainly: the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn. To hold it, I think, is as hard as holding the wind. And Krishna doesn't argue. That's the surprise. He says: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold. He agrees. Then he gives two words. By abhyasa and by vairagya, it can be held. Abhyasa: practice, doing it again and again. Vairagya: detachment, the fading of the pull, not letting every passing want drag you off. You need both. Practice alone becomes grim effort against a mind that keeps being yanked away. Detachment alone never builds the habit. Together they work like two oars. Verse thirty-six closes it: yoga is hard for the one who doesn't hold themselves, but for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. That's today's word, the mind is restless. True. And not the end of the story.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.` · `AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `KRISHNA AGREES.` · `PRACTICE AND DETACHMENT.` · then, large: `TWO OARS.`

segments.voice: Two oars, for two minutes. Sit, and pick one thing to rest on: the breath at the nose. That's the practice: coming back to it. When the mind runs off, and it will, notice where it ran. Don't chase the thought or argue with it. Just let the pull fade a little, and come back. Pull on both oars: return, and let go. Return, and let go. The bell holds the time.

Abhyasa. Practice, repeated effort, paired with vairagya, detachment. Arjuna's honest complaint, Gita six, thirty-four: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Krishna agrees: by practice and detachment it can be held.
Your line: practice and detachment. Today, when your mind runs off, don't take it as failure. Take it as one more stroke of the oar. Day one hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 181 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE WHO FELL SHORT.`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often pair abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (detachment) as the two supports of meditation; the Yoga Sutra names the same pair, and some practitioners return to Gita 6.34–35 when meditation feels impossible.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. Arjuna says his mind is as hard to hold as the wind. what do you say?
options: you're right. by practice and detachment it can be held.
fork.reveal: Krishna agrees first, then answers: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and detachment.

original.note: Sanskrit: abhyasa, practice, repeated effort; paired in 6.35 with vairagya, detachment.

trapdoor: what you thought: good meditators have quiet minds.
what it means: everyone's mind is restless; Krishna agrees, and gives two oars, practice and detachment.

what a scholar hears: 6.35's pair, abhyasa and vairagya, also appears in Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 1.12 as the means of stilling the mind; Arjuna's complaint opens with 'chanchalam hi manah', the mind is restless (6.34).
